Header:
Date: 2026-03-05 15:30 UTC

Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood Perf Eng), Emma Lawson (Orion CTO), Ravi Patel (Orion Platform Eng), Sofia Gomez (Orion MLE), Marcus Lee (Orion Security)

Summary: high-level runbook for replay-driven benchmarking to produce apples-to-apples comparisons across hosted/dedicated/private; focus areas: workload replay fidelity, KV cache warmup protocol, batching/batch shaping, quantization profiles, VPC/network egress effects. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics covered: workload replay design, prompt set construction, load generation tooling, latency SLO alignment, KV cache priming strategies, autoscaler behavior during bursts, network egress and VPC hop effects, security questionnaire and SOC2 artifact exchange.

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, automated transcript, medium quality)
[00:00:03] Ava: alright everyone thanks for joining, this is Ava from Redwood, i'm the account lead on this. we've got liam and priya with me, liam will run most of the benchmarking playbook and priya will talk perf knobs. can you hear me ok?
[00:00:12] Emma: yes, loud and clear, thanks for organising. we're mainly here to nail down how we'll run a replay load and make sure results are comparable to what we have on-prem.
[00:00:22] Liam: cool. quick agenda — replay harness and seed prompts, baseline configs (fp32), quantized runs, kv cache priming, batch shaping, network/VPC considerations, measurement surfaces and what a fair apples-to-apples means in our case.
[00:00:37] Ravi: sounds good. our big constraint is that customer infra has a lot of short requests — 60% sub-150 token — and we also have a long-tail of long context editorial tasks. so any batching needs to keep p95 under 250ms.
[00:00:54] Priya: noted. that distribution matters a lot for kernel selection and batching. we should capture real request size histogram — not just average — in the replay.
[00:01:05] Sofia: quick Q — when you say replay, are we talking exact request timing, or just request mix? we also have user IDs in the traces — we'll need to anonymize.
[00:01:15] Liam: good question. our recommended approach is two-phase: 1) a fidelity replay that preserves inter-arrival times and concurrency (to exercise autoscaler), and 2) a steady-state synthetic mix for longer runs to measure unit-cost. we accept anonymized payloads.
[00:01:31] Marcus: security-wise we need to know where logs live and whether payloads are stored after the run.
[00:01:36] Ava: Marcus, we'll send the security playbook. by default Redwood hosted ephemeral logs are retained 24h for debugging and can be disabled for the run; dedicated/private runs can have logging disabled and use customer KMS.
[00:01:50] Emma: okay that helps. can we outline the KV cache warmup protocol? our app uses a lot of conversational context reuse.
[00:01:58] Priya: yes — we propose a two-step kv priming: i) passive warming during a ramp phase where you replay real sessions to populate prefixes, ii) an explicit priming pass where we replay a curated set of high-reuse prompts to fully populate the KV entries for the benchmark. we'll record hit-rate over time.
[00:02:18] Ravi: how many passes typically? our cache is big but churn is high.
[00:02:24] Priya: usually 2–3 passes across the hot set; we'll measure hit-rate delta between pass 1 and pass 3 and use pass 3 as the benchmark start. note that quantization can change cache footprint, which affects eviction behavior.
[00:02:38] Liam: and that matters because if you compare an fp32 run with a 4-bit run and the cache hit rates differ, p95 might move just from cache churn. so apples-to-apples requires matching cache state as much as possible.
[00:02:52] Emma: interesting — so we need to record both token-level latency and cache metrics. can you confirm what counters Redwood exposes?
[00:02:59] Priya: sure — token latency histogram, per-request decomposition (kernel time, memcpy, enqueue/wait), kv cache hits/misses and evictions, batch size distribution, GPU utilization, GPU mem pressure, and network RTTs for VPC hops. we'll provide an export schema.
[00:03:16] Ava: we'll attach the export schema to the shared folder.
[00:03:20] [00:03:20] Sofia: will the replay harness emulate client retries and backoff? our prod sees a lot of 503 retries from legacy infra.
[00:03:28] Liam: the harness supports retry patterns; for apples-to-apples we recommend disabling synthetic retries unless you're explicitly testing retry behavior. instead we mirror the recorded retry behavior from your traces.
[00:03:40] Ravi: network — our on-prem has 2 VPC hops and 1 firewall appliance that adds about 20–30ms. how do you account for those when comparing to Redwood hosted?
[00:03:49] Priya: two ways: i) measure and report end-to-end latency including network, and ii) report service-side latency (server processing only) by stripping measured RTT. both figures will be published. for private/vpc we'll add measured egress/ingress RTTs to the report.
[00:04:06] Marcus: and encryption — our policy is customer-managed keys for model input in private mode. is that supported?
[00:04:11] Ava: yes, we support KMS integrations and HSM-based key wrapping on private deployments; for dedicated we can enable BYOK as well. we'll include the integration docs.
[00:04:20] [00:04:20] Emma: about batching — we saw earlier benchmarks where batching improved throughput but hurt p95 for small requests. how do you recommend shaping?
[00:04:28] Priya: batch shaping is workload-specific. for your short-request-heavy profile we recommend dynamic priority batching with a small max batch and a small latency threshold (e.g., max batch 16, wait 8ms). also use prefix caching so short-prefix hits avoid full kernel execution. we'll run a sweep of batch_size x wait_ms and produce a heatmap.
[00:04:47] Liam: to make the sweep reproducible across environments we fix RNG seeds, same model checkpoints, and same sequence-length distribution in the replay harness. that way differences are down to runtime and infra.
[00:04:58] Sofia: seeds — are there nondeterministic parts in the runtime (like kernel scheduling) that could still cause variance?
[00:05:05] Priya: yes, some nondet scheduling can cause jitter; we'll run multiple replicates and show variance bands. typically 5 replicates is enough to estimate p95 stability.
[00:05:15] Emma: what about quantization? we want to compare int8/4-bit vs fp32 to understand cost/latency tradeoffs.
[00:05:22] Priya: we'll run three profiles: baseline fp32, int8 (per-layer calibration), and 4-bit hybrid quant. each run will use the same primed cache and replay harness. note quantization can change logits slightly — we'll include a token-level similarity metric and simple downstream evals on a small prompt set to show quality delta.
[00:05:40] Marcus: are you able to run customer-run quantized builds in our VPC motif?
[00:05:44] Liam: for Private deployments we can run quant builds in your VPC; for hosted/dedicated we'll run Redwood-managed quant builds but can share build scripts for you to reproduce locally.
[00:05:54] [00:05:54] Ravi: curious about multi-model fallbacks — in production we sometimes fallback to a smaller model when load spikes. do you simulate tiered routing?
[00:06:02] Liam: yes — in the replay harness we can encode routing policies so during a capacity breach requests are routed to fallback models. we'll also test a policy that keeps p95 under SLO by shedding optional tokens (truncate or approximate).
[00:06:14] Emma: helpful. on the topic of metrics, can we get per-route cost breakdown (per-token GPU time, memory footprint) for each run?
[00:06:21] Priya: yes, we'll produce per-route/per-model cost estimates using token processing time and GPU hours. for apples-to-apples we normalize to the same GPU instance type where applicable.
[00:06:32] Sofia: ok, practical question — what's the minimum run length to get stable p95 numbers? 1 hour? 24 hours?
[00:06:39] Priya: for p95 on bursty workloads we recommend at least 2 hours of steady-state replay after priming, with multiple replicates. for cost/unit throughput a 24h synthetic run is useful but not required.
[00:06:50] Liam: we'll propose a 3-phase plan in the runbook: ramp+prime (30–45min), steady-state replica runs (2 hours x 3), and optional 24h cost run.
[00:07:01] [00:07:01] Emma: let's talk about measurement alignment — we can't change our in-app client instrumentation. can we map your export schema to our traces?
[00:07:09] Liam: yes — we'll share a mapping doc for your trace fields to Redwood counters. the harness will accept your timestamps and attach our stage timestamps so you can cross-validate.
[00:07:20] Marcus: on compliance, will the dedicated run require any additional attestation?
[00:07:24] Ava: dedicated customers get a tailored compliance packet; we'll attach SOC2 and encryption docs. if you need ISO/PCI templates we can raise a request.
[00:07:33] Ravi: about autoscaling behavior — we worry about cold-starts during bursty traffic. how are cold starts measured?
[00:07:39] Priya: we instrument cold-start latency by detecting the first request that triggers a new worker and tagging subsequent setup time (model load, warm JIT/compiles). we'll show cold-start percentiles and recommend pre-warming strategies or reserve capacity.
[00:07:52] Liam: and for Dedicated we can reserve a minimum pool to bound cold-starts; for Hosted we recommend burst windows with warmers or scheduled preloads.
[00:08:02] Emma: can we produce a single consolidated PDF report with tables + graphs and raw CSVs?
[00:08:07] Ava: yes, deliverables: PDF report, raw CSV exports, replay harness, config files, priming playlist, and a short slide deck summarizing answers.
[00:08:16] [00:08:16] Sofia: any gotchas people should know from past benchmarks?
[00:08:19] Priya: watch out for hidden variables: different CUDA versions and drivers, small differences in environment (MIG vs non-MIG), and network NIC offload settings. also virtualization can change latency tails. we'll document the environment matrix.
[00:08:34] Liam: also quant build flags — if you mix different kernels for quant and fp32 you must note kernel provenance. we've seen teams accidentally compare a tuned fp32 build against a stock quant build which skews results.
[00:08:47] Emma: good to know. on practicalities — how do we schedule the dedicated slot? we have a maintenance window next weekend.
[00:08:54] Ava: we'll propose two windows in the shared calendar; the week of 2026-03-16 is our current target. Liam will post exact times.
[00:08:59] [00:08:59] Marcus: one more question — will any PII be sent to Redwood? our traces have hashed user ids and some free-text which can contain names.
[00:09:08] Liam: we recommend redaction on your side. our policy is we don't inspect payloads; for hosted runs we can provide an encrypted blob and run inside a shielded environment. we'll include redaction checklist.
[00:09:20] Emma: ok let's recap — from Orion: provide anonymized traces, define p95 SLO and priority routes; from Redwood: replay harness, priming playlist, baseline configs, and security docs. timeline is share artifacts this week and run in mid-March.
[00:09:35] Ava: yep that's the plan. anything else?
[00:09:38] Ravi: can you also include a small script to compute token similarity for the quant eval?
[00:09:42] Priya: sure — we'll add a script that computes token-level edit distance, logit divergence, and a small quality pass rate on your evaluation prompt set.
[00:09:51] Sofia: thanks — that should cover it.
[00:09:54] [00:09:54] Closing: quick timeline and owners review, then we'll send invites for the benchmark kickoff. thanks everyone.
